## In Layman's Terms

Changing a club changes the mechanical system the golfer moves. It can also change how the
golfer moves it. Simulation helps separate specified versions of these questions: what happens
under the same applied torque history, under the same feedback policy, or under the same handle
motion? Those are different experiments, with different quantities held fixed.

A repeatable simulation is valuable because its assumptions and calculations can be inspected.
It does not predict a person's response exactly. Camera errors, uncertain shaft properties,
unknown grip loads, imperfect contact models and adaptation can all change the observed result.
Good fitting therefore combines controlled measurements with models whose limits are explicit.

The chain is **geometry and material identification → flexible response → delivery state →
contact and ball flight → a fitting decision**. An error at an earlier link can appear as an
apparently convincing explanation at a later one. This article develops the mechanical links
and a proposed reporting structure; it does not report a validated fitting product or human trial.

## Why This Article Exists

A lower shot with a stiffer shaft could reflect different shaft deformation, changed handle
motion, a different strike location, measurement variation, or several of these together.
Launch data alone do not identify which explanation is responsible. A model makes alternatives
explicit and suggests additional measurements that can distinguish them.

The parameters include mass, center of mass, rotational inertia, shaft geometry, bending and
torsional stiffness, damping, grip boundary conditions and the contact model. Identifying all
of them from a few launch outcomes is generally underdetermined. Measure accessible properties
independently, examine parameter sensitivity and correlation, and reserve trials that were not
used for calibration to assess predictions.

::: {.callout-note title="Notation and Intervention Contract"}
For a declared effective plant, a control-affine representation may be written
$\dot x=f_p(x,t)+G_p(x,t)u$. State $x$ includes the chosen rigid, flexible and actuator states;
$p$ identifies model parameters. Explicit time permits a declared prescribed boundary motion.
Within a smooth mode, control-affine structure depends on the chosen input: muscle
activation, muscle force and joint torque are not interchangeable signals. Contact transitions
need separately declared event and reset laws.

A [Zero-Torque Counterfactual](zero-torque-counterfactual.html) sets the **declared applied
control channels** to zero. Gravity, passive elastic loads, retained actuators, contact reactions
and prescribed-boundary work do not vanish merely because those channels are zero. Replaying a
nonzero input on different equipment is an equipment counterfactual, not a zero-input trajectory.
The [Drift-Control Ratio](../NOTATION.md#dcr-and-dgcr) compares projected drift acceleration with
bounded control authority under a stated metric and admissible input set; it does not rank clubs
or identify adaptation on its own. See [the notation contract](../NOTATION.md).
:::

## Part I: Delivery Kinematics and Equipment Counterfactuals

### A Twist Requires Frames and a Reference Point

Immediately before contact, a rigid-head approximation has a pose and a velocity. A twist
supplies the velocity part; it does not contain the head's position, orientation, face shape
or contact point. Here all vectors are measured relative to an inertial world frame and
expressed in its axes. For a head-fixed point $A$, use angular-first ordering:

$$
\boldsymbol{\xi}_A=
\begin{pmatrix}\boldsymbol{\omega}\\\mathbf v_A\end{pmatrix}.
$$

This six-vector representation of rigid-body velocity is often called a twist; its relation
to an $\mathfrak{se}(3)$ matrix depends on the selected spatial/body convention.
For two points fixed in the same rigid head, let
$\mathbf r_{B/A}=\mathbf r_B-\mathbf r_A$ and define
$[\mathbf r]_\times\mathbf a=\mathbf r\times\mathbf a$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf v_B&=\mathbf v_A+\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_{B/A},\\
\boldsymbol\xi_B&=
\begin{pmatrix}I_3&0\\-[\mathbf{r}_{B/A}]_\times&I_3\end{pmatrix}
\boldsymbol\xi_A.
\end{aligned}
$$

The minus sign follows from $\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r=-\mathbf r\times\boldsymbol\omega$.
For $\boldsymbol\omega=(0,0,2)$ rad/s and $\mathbf r_{B/A}=(0.3,0,0)$ m, the added
velocity is $(0,0.6,0)$ m/s. This is a point shift with unchanged axes, not a general
rotation-and-translation frame change. Drake explicitly distinguishes the measured-in frame,
expressed-in frame and reference point [@drakeSpatialVelocity].

Wrenches must use the dual shift. With force $\mathbf F$ and moment $\boldsymbol\tau_A$,
$\boldsymbol\tau_B=\boldsymbol\tau_A-\mathbf r_{B/A}\times\mathbf F$. Consequently,
$\boldsymbol\tau_A\cdot\boldsymbol\omega+\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v_A$
equals the corresponding power evaluated at $B$. Changing the point in a velocity record
without changing the moment reference can create a false energy-transfer claim.

### What Is Held Fixed?

Let the baseline model use parameters $p_0$, input history $u_0(t)$ and state $x_0(t)$.
At a declared branch time $t_b$, define an admissible initial-state map
$\Phi_{01}$ into candidate model $p_1$. Equal numerical coordinates are not necessarily the
same physical state when length, reference configuration, mass distribution or flexible
coordinates change. Position, velocity, strain and stored energy cannot always all be held
fixed simultaneously; record the choice and enforce the candidate's constraints.

An open-loop input replay is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\dot x_1&=f_{p_1}(x_1,t)+G_{p_1}(x_1,t)u_0(t),\\
x_1(t_b)&=\Phi_{01}(x_0(t_b)).
\end{aligned}
$$

Compare it with a baseline simulation using the same declared integration and initialization
policy. Baseline fit error against measured motion must be reported separately. The replay
isolates a parameter intervention **within that model**, conditional on the frozen input,
initial-state mapping and retained loads. The input may be estimated rather than measured;
inverse dynamics identifies net generalized loads only under its own model and external-force
assumptions. It does not uniquely recover muscle activations.

Other questions require other interventions:

- **Same feedback policy:** $u_1(t)=\pi(x_1(t),t)$. The policy is fixed, but its numerical
  output generally changes as the state changes. This differs from open-loop replay.
- **Same handle motion:** prescribe a measured pose trajectory at the grip and solve for
  shaft/head response and reaction loads. Input work can change. Prescribing all handle
  motions and all conjugate loads independently generally overconstrains the boundary.
- **Zero declared control:** integrate the specified zero-input model. A retained moving
  grip can still supply energy, and initial shaft strain can still release energy.

At a fixed diagnostic time $t_f$, compare delivery twists at the same named geometric
reference convention and in common axes. Club-specific centers of mass are different
physical points, so their speeds are not automatically a face-center comparison. For actual
impact, each branch must instead locate its own valid contact event. The candidate can arrive
earlier, later, at a different face location, or miss the ball; evaluating both at the old
impact time does not ensure that both are impacting.

An observed-minus-predicted residual is not an identified neural adaptation. It also contains
measurement error, parameter uncertainty, initial-state mismatch, unmodeled loads and numerical
error. Repeated, appropriately controlled trials and additional measurements are needed to
study adaptation. Determinism makes a model replay auditable; it does not remove those alternatives.

## Part II: Flexible Shaft Dynamics

### Bending and Torsion Have Different Equations

Let $s\in[0,L]$ denote the undeformed shaft coordinate. For one small transverse displacement
$w(s,t)$ about a declared reference motion, a bounded Euler–Bernoulli model with prescribed
axial tension $N(s,t)$ is

$$
\lambda w_{tt}+(EIw_{ss})_{ss}-(Nw_s)_s=q.
$$

Here $\lambda$ is mass per length in kg/m, $EI$ is bending rigidity in N·m², $N$ is axial
force in N, and $q$ is transverse load per length in N/m. Every term is a force density.
A second bending direction needs its own rigidity and coordinates; anisotropic composite
shafts may also require coupling terms. Euler–Bernoulli theory neglects shear deformation.
Timoshenko theory introduces an independent section rotation, shear stiffness and rotary
inertia; these names do not describe one interchangeable equation [@delftBeam].

For a small Saint-Venant torsional angle $\theta(s,t)$, a separate simple model is

$$
\mu_\theta\theta_{tt}-(GJ\theta_s)_s=m_s.
$$

$\mu_\theta=\int_A\rho r_\perp^2\,dA$ is polar mass moment per length in kg·m;
$GJ$ is effective torsional rigidity in N·m²; $m_s$ is applied torque per length in N·m/m.
For a noncircular or anisotropic section, the appropriate effective torsional rigidity is
not obtained by blindly substituting the geometric polar second moment.
Applying the bending operator and translational mass density to $\theta$ is dimensionally wrong.

These equations are explanatory linearizations. A moving, rotating base requires consistent
transport/inertial terms; large bending, bend–twist coupling, damping, gravity, grip compliance
and head boundary inertia may require a richer formulation. The tip is not a free unloaded
end when a clubhead is attached. Initial conditions, grip conditions and force/moment balance
at the hosel close the model. Boundary excitation must not be counted twice in $q$ and the
prescribed motion.

### A Centrifugal-Load Check

Consider only a straight radial shaft rotating steadily at angular speed $\Omega$, with its
root at radius $R_0$ and a point head mass $m_h$ at $R_0+L$. Its tensile preload is

$$
\begin{aligned}
N(s)&=\Omega^2\int_s^L\lambda(\sigma)(R_0+\sigma)\,d\sigma\\
&\quad+\Omega^2m_h(R_0+L).
\end{aligned}
$$

The acceleration is proportional to radius, not radius squared. Integrating $\lambda v^2$
over length gives energy units, not force. For the synthetic values $\lambda=0.06$ kg/m,
$L=1.1$ m, $R_0=0.2$ m, $\Omega=40$ rad/s and $m_h=0.2$ kg, the base load is
$79.2+416=495.2$ N. This is a dimensional/numerical example, not a measured swing load or a
formula for an arbitrarily oriented, accelerating golf shaft.

Lead/lag, droop and twist describe components in a declared shaft or delivery frame, not fixed
world directions throughout the swing. A force whose line of action passes through the head
center of mass contributes $\mathbf M=\mathbf r_{CG/hosel}\times\mathbf F$ about the hosel.
Other forces use their actual application points; any free couples must be added. The component
in the selected bending plane depends on both vectors. An offset alone does not establish a toe-down angle.
Lead need not always add loft, and torsion need not always delay face rotation: mapping
shaft deformation into delivered face orientation depends on pose, mounting and the excitation
history. No universal acceleration, droop or twist ranges are established here.

### Discretization Must Preserve Coupling

A collection of diagonal springs is not automatically equivalent to a beam. For a uniform
Euler–Bernoulli segment of length $\ell$, clamp one end and use tip displacement $w$ and
slope $\phi=dw/ds$ with their conjugate transverse force and moment. The remaining stiffness is

$$
\begin{pmatrix}F\\M\end{pmatrix}
=\frac{EI}{\ell^3}
\begin{pmatrix}12&-6\ell\\-6\ell&4\ell^2\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}w\\\phi\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The off-diagonal terms are essential. With zero tip moment, solving both equations gives
$w=F\ell^3/(3EI)$ and $\phi=F\ell^2/(2EI)$. Keeping only the translational diagonal gives
$F\ell^3/(12EI)$, four times too small for that boundary condition. If tip rotation is
instead constrained, the diagonal translation result answers that different experiment.
The complete two-node beam element retains both ends and their coupling [@delftStiffness].

Similarly, uniform static torsion gives $\theta=ML/(GJ)$ and stored energy
$GJ\theta^2/(2L)$. These limits are useful tests before simulating a swing. Select element
count through convergence of delivery quantities, modes and energy balance; a fixed count
such as 10–20 does not certify accuracy. Compare time-step refinement and damping models as
well. Equivalent static stiffness alone does not ensure equivalent dynamic response.

## Part III: Geometry, Density and Inertia

### What a Watertight Mesh Can Establish

A consistently oriented, closed, non-self-intersecting mesh can define a polyhedral material
region. An exterior scan alone usually does not identify wall thickness, cavities, internal
weights or density. A hollow multimaterial head needs those regions and material assignments;
watertightness alone does not reveal its mass distribution. Exact integration of a specified
polyhedron is also distinct from exact knowledge of the manufactured part or curved CAD surface.

The divergence theorem reduces polynomial volume moments to surface integrals. Eberly's
primary derivation explains this reduction and its constant-density assumptions
[@eberlyMass]. The following signed-tetrahedron form provides a compact independent check.
For each outward-oriented triangular face with vertices $\mathbf a_k,\mathbf b_k,\mathbf c_k$
expressed from a common origin, define

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta V_k=\frac{1}{6}\mathbf a_k\cdot(\mathbf b_k\times\mathbf c_k),\\
V=\sum_k\Delta V_k,\qquad m=\rho V,\\
\mathbf r_{CG}=\frac{1}{4V}\sum_k\Delta V_k
(\mathbf a_k+\mathbf b_k+\mathbf c_k).
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the centroid numerator written directly in scalar triple products carries $1/24$,
not $1/4$. Individual signed volumes may be negative if the origin lies outside the body;
taking their absolute values separately corrupts the integral. Cavity boundaries must have
the orientation appropriate to the material region. Check manifold closure, units and
orientation before interpreting the result; nearly cancelling terms may require a better
origin or numerical summation strategy.

The unit tetrahedron with vertices $0,\mathbf e_x,\mathbf e_y,\mathbf e_z$ has
$V=1/6$ and centroid $(1/4,1/4,1/4)$. These identities immediately detect the earlier
factor errors. They also remain valid after translating the whole tetrahedron and its centroid.

For a density field $\rho(\mathbf r)$ and an origin $O$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_O&=\int_\Omega\rho(\mathbf r)
\left(\|\mathbf r\|^2I_3-\mathbf r\mathbf r^T\right)dV,\\
I_{CG}&=I_O-m\left(\|\mathbf r_{CG}\|^2I_3
-\mathbf r_{CG}\mathbf r_{CG}^T\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

Off-diagonal tensor entries are the negatives of the corresponding product integrals.
For the unit tetrahedron at unit density, $I_{CG}$ has diagonal entries $1/80$ and
off-diagonal entries $1/480$, in the consistent chosen length/mass units. A tensor must be
symmetric and physically realizable; nonnegative eigenvalues alone are insufficient because
principal moments must also satisfy the triangle inequalities.

### Assemblies Must Share Axes

For component masses $m_j$, centers $\mathbf c_j$ in common assembly axes, and rotations $R_j$
from component principal/local axes into assembly axes, first find
$\mathbf c=\sum_jm_j\mathbf c_j/\sum_jm_j$. Then, with $\mathbf d_j=\mathbf c_j-\mathbf c$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
J_j&=R_jI_{C_j}^{(j)}R_j^T,\\
P(\mathbf d)&=\|\mathbf d\|^2I_3-\mathbf d\mathbf d^T,\\
I_C&=\sum_j\left[J_j+m_jP(\mathbf d_j)\right].
\end{aligned}
$$

Omitting $R_j$ silently assumes every component tensor already uses the same axes.
Avoid double-counting overlapping material domains. Density is a measured or specified input,
not a universal material-name constant. Validate total mass and center of mass against the
assembled club and, where possible, validate inertia independently. A normalized mesh that
matches total mass can still place that mass incorrectly.

## Part IV: Proposed Equipment Data

The next three JSON blocks are **proposed data examples**, not published wire standards.
The earlier `golf-club/fitting-document/v1`, `swing-sim/delivery-trajectory/v1` and
`golf-club/fitting-report/v1` names did not have matching schemas or implementations in this
repository. These examples therefore omit schema URLs and compatibility guarantees.
All identities and numbers below are synthetic; they are not OEM specifications, measured
player records, qualified engine runs or purchase recommendations.

A future equipment contract should identify geometry/material artifacts, measurement methods,
uncertainty, cut versus uncut shaft state, mounting transforms, stiffness/damping profiles and
versioned unit conventions. Here a short SI example illustrates consistent axis naming:

```json
{
  "example_status": "synthetic_not_a_validated_run",
  "proposal": "equipment_record",
  "equipment_id": "example_club_A",
  "head_frame": {
    "origin": "head_center_of_mass",
    "axes": "orthonormal right-handed; x face normal, y selected heel-toe direction, z=x cross y"
  },
  "head": {
    "mass_kg": 0.1985,
    "cg_from_hosel_expressed_in_head_m": [0.0382, 0.0145, -0.0128],
    "inertia_about_cg_expressed_in_head_kg_m2": [
      [0.000485, -0.0000085, 0.000012],
      [-0.0000085, 0.000312, -0.0000045],
      [0.000012, -0.0000045, 0.000541]
    ]
  },
  "shaft": {
    "state": "cut_and_prepared_for_this_example",
    "length_m": 1.143,
    "mass_kg": 0.0621,
    "stiffness_and_damping_profile": null,
    "profile_status": "not_supplied_not_simulation_ready"
  }
}
```

The earlier g·cm² unit converts by $1\ \mathrm{g\,cm^2}=10^{-7}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}$.
Here the physical direction of the positive heel-toe axis must be selected consistently with
the stated right-handed construction and the particular club. Do not independently label an
inconsistent third axis “up.” An actual schema must specify missing-value behavior and reject
incomplete records for simulation. A single shaft frequency does not identify its full mass,
stiffness and damping distributions.

## Part V: Proposed Delivery Records and Engine Comparisons

A trajectory record supports comparison but cannot reconstruct the governing model by itself.
Exchange the model, actuator and constraint definitions, flexible discretization, initialization,
input policy, contact parameters, integrator and solver settings as well. Record engine version,
platform and numerical tolerances. MuJoCo's model compiler and contact/constraint options are
examples of backend-specific choices that a label such as “compatible” does not settle
[@mujocoModeling]. Cross-engine agreement needs executable comparison cases and reported errors;
bitwise identity is a separate, usually much stricter requirement.

```json
{
  "example_status": "synthetic_not_a_validated_run",
  "proposal": "delivery_excerpt",
  "equipment_ref": "example_club_A",
  "engine_run": null,
  "world_axes": "orthonormal right-handed; x lateral, y target, z up",
  "pose_convention": "head-to-world rotation; head origin at center of mass",
  "velocity_measured_in": "world",
  "velocity_expressed_in": "world",
  "velocity_reference_point": "head_center_of_mass",
  "time_reference": "declared diagnostic instant; contact not established",
  "sampling_status": "two illustrative samples; no integration step implied",
  "trajectory_samples": [
    {
      "time_s": -0.05,
      "position_world_m": [0.124, -0.45, 1.25],
      "orientation_quaternion_wxyz": [1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0],
      "angular_velocity_world_rad_s": [12.4, 5.8, 18.2],
      "cg_velocity_world_m_s": [14.2, 28.5, -8.4],
      "shaft_coordinates": {"lead_m": -0.0184, "droop_m": -0.0121, "twist_rad": -0.0314}
    },
    {
      "time_s": 0.0,
      "position_world_m": [0.0, 0.0, 0.025],
      "orientation_quaternion_wxyz": [0.8, 0.0, 0.6, 0.0],
      "angular_velocity_world_rad_s": [22.8, 8.4, 48.6],
      "cg_velocity_world_m_s": [1.4, 48.2, 4.1],
      "shaft_coordinates": {"lead_m": 0.0246, "droop_m": -0.0282, "twist_rad": 0.0070}
    }
  ]
}
```

The quaternions are unit length and their mapping direction is named. Their samples and
velocities have not been integrated into a dynamically consistent trajectory. A production
validator must distinguish such a structural example from usable motion: verify temporal
ordering, quaternion/velocity consistency, reference-point transforms, interpolation and
contact events. The shaft coordinates also need a fully specified moving basis, sign convention
and reference configuration before use. Sparse reporting times are not solver time steps.

## Part VI: Reproducible Reports and Statistical Meaning

A deterministic forward run produces an output conditional on inputs and model choices.
Dispersion requires an ensemble: repeated measured swings, a declared input distribution,
parameter uncertainty or some combination. Report which variation was sampled and which
uncertainties were omitted. Separate validation data from calibration data.

A 95% confidence interval for a population mean is not a 95% interval for individual shots.
For an illustrative independent normal sample with **known** standard deviation $\sigma=4.2$ m
and $n=25$, the mean interval half-width is approximately $1.96\sigma/\sqrt n=1.6464$ m.
The central interval about the known population mean for individual outcomes has half-width
$1.96\sigma=8.232$ m. With estimated parameters, dependence or non-normal outcomes, use and
describe an appropriate method; do not attach “95%” to an unexplained dispersion number.

```json
{
  "example_status": "synthetic_not_a_validated_run",
  "proposal": "fitting_report",
  "equipment_ref": "example_club_A",
  "candidate_delivery_and_launch": null,
  "uncertainty_example": {
    "model": "independent normal observations with known standard deviation",
    "sample_count": 25,
    "known_carry_standard_deviation_m": 4.2,
    "normal_quantile_approximation": 1.96,
    "mean_confidence_interval_half_width_m": 1.6464,
    "population_central_interval_half_width_m": 8.232
  },
  "sensitivity_estimates": null,
  "physical_validation": "not_performed",
  "recommendation": "withheld_pending_identification_and_validation"
}
```

Sensitivity gradients must name their input units and intervention. A derivative with respect
to “shaft EI per unit” is ambiguous for a spatial profile: define, for example, a dimensionless
scale multiplying a fixed profile, and state which other parameters are held fixed. Perturbing
head mass at fixed geometry also changes inertia unless a different artificial intervention is
explicitly intended. Contact-event changes can make a local derivative discontinuous or
inapplicable. Check step-size dependence before interpreting it as a design direction.

Delivery twist alone cannot determine launch. Relative contact velocity, face normal, strike
location, ball properties, friction, face/ball compliance and the chosen contact law also enter.
A scalar restitution parameter is an effective model input under defined conditions, not a
universal material constant or equipment-conformance certificate. Carry adds aerodynamic and
environmental assumptions. Optimality is therefore conditional on a declared objective, player
population, constraints and uncertainty, rather than the largest simulated carry number.

## Part VII: Verification Architecture

Start with independent checks at each link. Test signed-volume integration on analytic solids,
verify frame shifts with power invariance, and check static bending/torsion limits before dynamic
simulation. Establish convergence and energy balance, then compare predicted shaft motion and
head delivery with measurements that were not used to fit the parameters. Test the impact and
flight models against their own evidence rather than allowing their error to be absorbed into
shaft stiffness. Finally assess repeatability and player response in a controlled fitting study.

These checks connect the article's central questions. A center-of-mass error changes both the
inertial loading and the conversion from center-of-mass velocity to face-point velocity.
An omitted beam coupling changes deformation and reaction work. A shifted impact time changes
which delivery state enters the collision model. Treating the resulting prediction residual as
neural adaptation would hide all three mechanical alternatives.

The useful outcome is an inspectable chain of conditional predictions and tests. Empirical
fitting supplies essential evidence for that chain; simulation helps identify what to measure
and which explanations remain distinguishable.
